title: Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss

concept.text: The proposed innovation is regeneration of durable, voluntarily controlled, force-producing skeletal muscle after substantial volumetric muscle loss (VML). It would replace missing contractile tissue with living muscle that receives adequate blood flow, responds to motor nerves and transmits force through appropriate mechanical attachments. Success would require coordinated restoration of muscle mass, structure and function.

VML can leave persistent losses of muscle mass and contractile strength because endogenous regeneration does not adequately replace the missing tissue. Fibrosis, vascular abnormalities and disrupted innervation complicate recovery. The intended capability would overcome these interacting limitations sufficiently to restore useful voluntary force; the supplied evidence does not establish that this has been achieved in humans after substantial VML.

significance.text: Restoring substantial muscle mass and voluntary force without sacrificing donor muscle would represent a major reconstructive capability beyond the modest clinical recovery described in the supplied evidence. Persistent weakness is a central consequence of VML, so durable strength restoration would directly address the injury's functional burden. The advance would be meaningful because the regenerated tissue contracts and contributes force, rather than merely occupying the defect.

Conditional applications: restored muscle force could improve gait, increase the usefulness of a salvaged limb, provide power for a tendon transfer or improve residual-limb function. These outcomes would also depend on the location of the defect, mechanical attachments, neural control, rehabilitation and other injuries. They are plausible downstream possibilities, not automatic consequences or demonstrated outcomes of the proposed innovation.

Scope synthesis: this capability would address one major component of limb function. It would not by itself establish regeneration of an amputated extremity, restoration of a destroyed joint or repair of a transected nerve trunk. Those distinctions limit how broadly successful muscle regeneration could be interpreted, especially in injuries involving several tissues.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated regeneration of enough functional muscle to restore durable voluntary force after a substantial tissue deficit. The barriers extend beyond generating muscle cells: viable contractile tissue must develop an effective architecture, receive adequate perfusion, acquire motor innervation and transmit its force to the remaining musculoskeletal system. Damage to nerves, vessels and myotendinous junctions varies between injuries, so the integration problem will also vary.

The injured environment itself can obstruct regeneration. The supplied review describes impaired extracellular-matrix remodeling that suppresses satellite-cell activation, alongside fibrosis, vascular dysfunction and denervation. Satellite cells therefore cannot be assumed to rebuild a large defect simply because they participate in normal muscle repair. A successful treatment would need to overcome the local conditions that prevent effective regeneration while establishing functional tissue integration.

The evidence does not establish a universal defect-size threshold above which muscle invariably heals with fibrosis. It also does not substantiate the original assertion about donor-site limitations of transferred muscle flaps. Avoiding donor-muscle sacrifice remains a proposed design objective, but the supplied record cannot quantify the comparative advantage over flap reconstruction.

current_state.text: Garg and colleagues' review, published online on 28 February 2025 in the Journal of Physiology, volume 603, pages 7421–7439, DOI 10.1113/JP286551, reports that only acellular extracellular-matrix scaffolds had been combined with physical therapy in VML-injured patients, with modest functional improvement. That statement concerns the scaffold-plus-physical-therapy approach described in the abstract; it does not establish that patients had received no other kinds of treatment. The supplied evidence for this article is a PubMed abstract record, not the full review, despite its untruncated extraction.

Sarah M. Greising and Jarrod A. Call's review was first published on 20 November 2025 and appeared in Experimental Physiology, volume 111, pages 1718–1732, in 2026, DOI 10.1113/EP093074. It describes persistent deficits after VML, partial preclinical recovery and continuing translational limitations, and states that full functional recovery remains elusive. The supplied validated review reports that the retained full-text XML identifies both authors and includes the article body and references without reported truncation, resolving the earlier incomplete author capture.

Together, these dated reviews support a continuing gap between partial recovery and durable restoration of reinnervated human muscle force after substantial VML. The supplied material does not document the earlier assertion that rat constructs produced early force gains that later converged with controls. That trajectory remains unverified here; its absence from this record does not establish that the underlying result is false.

Temporal limitation: the supplied bounded search record is empty. These sources support statements at their documented review dates, but they do not establish an exhaustive account of developments through 1 November 2026 or prove that no subsequent breakthrough occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human demonstration: enroll patients with an acute, prospectively defined substantial volumetric defect of a major limb muscle, such as the quadriceps. At two years, treatment would restore viable contractile muscle volume and voluntary torque to within a proposed 15% of an appropriate reference, demonstrate reinnervation by electromyography and avoid donor-muscle sacrifice. The 15% tolerance, two-year duration, acute setting and donor-sparing condition are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Two-year contractile volume and voluntary torque recover within 15%

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement safeguards: define defect size, reference measurements and rehabilitation before treatment. Distinguish viable contractile tissue from fibrotic or other space-filling tissue, demonstrate adequate perfusion and show that the restored tissue contributes to mechanical force transmission. Torque recovery should be evaluated for compensation by surviving muscle. Contralateral measurements should be interpreted alongside preinjury measurements where available and suitable external reference data.
completion_criteria.label: Measurements verify perfused contractile tissue contributes to force transmission

completion_criteria.text: The rationale for prioritizing force, mass, structure and reinnervation follows from the documented deficits and the review's emphasis on contraction and force production as the principal function of muscle. The review's caution about contralateral controls concerned mouse mitochondrial respiration; it supports careful reference selection but does not itself invalidate human contralateral torque comparisons.
completion_criteria.label: Mouse respiration cautions do not invalidate human contralateral torque comparisons

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce substantial functional restoration in independent patient cohorts with clearly described defect locations, sizes, associated injuries and rehabilitation. Report durability, safety and the conditions under which recovery fails or remains incomplete. A scaffold that fills space and produces only a small strength gain would not meet this proposed endpoint. Success in an acute quadriceps defect would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested conditions; chronic scarred defects, other muscles and injuries with major nerve or attachment loss would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent patient cohorts reproduce functional restoration with reported practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, encompasses a much broader reconstruction problem in which functional muscle would be one necessary component. ORT-06 concerns replacement of missing muscle within an existing limb and would not establish whole-limb regeneration. ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps, overlaps through the need for effective neural control, but muscle reinnervation does not demonstrate repair across a long nerve gap or recovery of sensory function.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis, concerns the attachment through which tendon transfers load to bone. ORT-06 needs effective force transmission, but generating contractile muscle would not by itself regenerate an injured enthesis. ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, addresses a separate joint-level barrier to limb function. ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, shares the broad goal of functional tissue restoration while targeting a different anatomical structure and mechanical role.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, could complement muscle reconstruction in a combined bone-and-muscle defect. ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, concerns control of bone formation rather than muscle regeneration. ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate, targets skeletal growth. Success in any one of these capabilities would not establish the others.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction, could matter when muscle reconstruction accompanies an infected orthopedic injury. Its defining endpoint is infection eradication while retaining the reconstruction; ORT-06's defining endpoint is regenerated muscle force. The capabilities remain distinct even when both are needed in the same patient.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not verify the claimed early-to-late convergence of rat construct force gains with controls.
Developments after the dated reviews, including the latest state as of 1 November 2026, remain unverified.
A universal defect-size threshold and the asserted donor-site limitations of muscle-flap reconstruction are not established by the supplied record.
The proposed human endpoint still requires protocol-specific definitions of substantial defect size, viable contractile volume, reference values and attribution of recovered force.
The proposed 15% tolerance and two-year duration have not been established here as consensus thresholds.
Benefits for gait, tendon transfers and residual limbs remain conditional applications requiring direct evaluation.
Related-concept comparisons rely on the supplied roster titles rather than detailed evidence reviews of those entries.

brief.title: Regrowing missing muscle that restores strength
possible: People who have lost a large amount of muscle to injury could regain lasting strength they control voluntarily. New living muscle would replace the missing tissue, receive blood and nerve signals, and pull through working attachments.
Depending on the injury, restored strength could help someone walk, use a salvaged limb or improve the function of a remaining limb after amputation.
why: Large muscle injuries can leave lasting weakness because the body cannot adequately replace what is missing. Restoring muscle that actually produces force would address that loss directly.
A treatment that avoids taking muscle from elsewhere in the body would offer another way to rebuild strength after severe injury.

sources.showed: Their review reports modest functional improvements in patients treated with cell-free scaffolds, supporting frameworks made from material around cells, alongside physical therapy.
sources.quote: To date, only acellular extracellular matrix scaffolds have been combined with physical therapy in VML-injured patients, resulting in modest improvements in functional recovery.
sources.cited_for: It supports the clinical starting point: modest recovery from scaffolds combined with rehabilitation.
sources.not_established: It does not establish durable restoration of voluntarily controlled strength after substantial muscle loss.

sources.who: Sarah M. Greising and Jarrod A. Call
sources.showed: Their review describes persistent weakness, scar tissue, disrupted blood supply and lost nerve connections after major muscle loss. It reports that full functional recovery remains elusive.
sources.quote: Impaired extracellular matrix remodelling suppresses muscle stem cell (i.e., satellite cell) activation, further blocking the ability of the cell to self‐regenerate.
sources.cited_for: It explains why replacing muscle requires restoring its blood supply, nerve connections and ability to produce force.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate complete, lasting restoration of human muscle strength.

shown: Garg and colleagues describe modest clinical recovery with scaffolds and physical therapy. Greising and Call describe partial recovery in preclinical studies, but full functional recovery remains elusive.
missing: People have yet to regain lasting voluntary strength from enough newly regenerated muscle after a substantial loss.
Restored tissue must combine working muscle structure, adequate blood flow, nerve control and attachments that transmit force.
Measurements must distinguish force from new muscle from compensation by surviving muscle.
Independent patient groups must reproduce recovery, with clear accounts of safety, durability and failures.

milestones.label: Lasting recovery of muscle volume and voluntary strength
milestones.explanation: An acute major-limb injury trial would need lasting muscle-volume and joint-turning-force recovery within 15% of reference, nerve-test evidence of restored connections and no donor muscle sacrifice. This would establish useful human recovery.

milestones.label: New muscle receives blood and transmits force
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to distinguish living muscle from scar tissue and show blood flow and force transmission, using predefined comparisons and rehabilitation. This would establish that new muscle contributes to recovered strength.

milestones.label: Opposite-limb strength comparisons have a sound basis
milestones.explanation: Human comparisons would need suitable reference values; cautions about cellular oxygen use in mice do not themselves invalidate opposite-limb force comparisons. This matters because recovery needs a sound benchmark.

milestones.label: Independent patient groups reproduce recovery and define its limits
milestones.explanation: Independent patient groups would have to reproduce substantial, lasting recovery while reporting safety, injury details, rehabilitation and failures. This would establish where treatment works and where recovery remains incomplete.

uncertain: The proposed recovery tolerance and follow-up duration are evaluation choices, rather than agreed standards.
Trials still need precise definitions of substantial muscle loss, viable muscle volume and appropriate reference values.
Success in a fresh thigh injury would leave open whether treatment works in chronic scars or injuries with major nerve or attachment loss.

page.title: Functional skeletal muscle regeneration after volumetric muscle loss
page.definition: Skeletal muscle lost after injury is regenerated as living tissue that receives blood and motor-nerve signals and transmits force under voluntary control. Volumetric muscle loss is a tissue deficit that exceeds the muscle's capacity to regenerate.

goal.need: Human VML treatment must replace missing tissue as well as improve strength. In the cohort below, tissue loss and strength gain used different denominators; the gain did not establish restoration to an uninjured limb or show that new muscle caused it. A review published online on 28 February 2025 describes modest clinical functional recovery with scaffolds and physical therapy.

figures.caption: Reported averages in a 13-patient VML cohort published on 21 July 2016.
figures.note: Patients received extracellular-matrix scaffolds and rehabilitation. The study had no untreated comparison group.

completion.title: Independent human studies demonstrate voluntary force from regenerated muscle after VML.
completion.criterion: A registered, controlled human study demonstrates that newly regenerated muscle within a VML defect contributes voluntary force, measured in newtons or joint torque in newton-metres, through its mechanical attachments at the protocol's final follow-up after rehabilitation. Perfusion and motor innervation are demonstrated, and the analysis distinguishes force from new tissue from compensation by surviving muscle. An independent human study reproduces this integrated result.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback criterion; no external integrated human muscle-regeneration test was located.
completion.basis: Searched ASTM F3645-25, USAMMDA/MTEC VML targets, NIAMS awards and ClinicalTrials.gov VML records for an integrated human regeneration endpoint, force-recovery percentage and durability interval; found none. ASTM states: “This guide is not intended to identify a standard of functional recovery.” This fallback tests the programmes' functional-muscle objective and requires independent confirmation.

milestones.title: Regenerated muscle in a mouse VML defect responds to nerve stimulation at 180 days.
milestones.criterion: New skeletal muscle identified within the repair site produces a compound muscle action potential, the electrical response to motor-nerve stimulation, recorded separately from surrounding healthy muscle. Sicari et al. demonstrated this in scaffold-treated mouse VML defects at 180 days; Figure 2 reports n=8. This establishes activation of innervated tissue without measuring its mechanical force.
milestones.set_by: University of Pittsburgh, Sicari et al. (2014), published mouse VML experimental protocol; 180 days is its study-specific endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: After nerve stimulation, ECM-treated VML defects showed muscle activation characteristics

milestones.title: An animal VML treatment increases electrically evoked torque over control treatment at P<0.05.
milestones.criterion: A regenerative treatment increases electrically evoked muscle torque relative to its control under the published experiment's statistical test. Clark et al. reported greater tetanic dorsiflexion torque after MyoD gene delivery than after mock delivery four weeks after rat VML injury; functional assays reported n=7 and used ANOVA with Tukey comparisons. The study's significance threshold was P<0.05. This is an experimental efficacy bar, not a threshold for normal muscle function.
milestones.set_by: Indiana University, Clark et al. (2022), published rat VML functional-testing and statistical-analysis protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the significance value being defined as p < 0.05.

milestones.title: A treated human VML muscle's motor response amplitude increases by at least 20%.
milestones.criterion: After human VML repair, motor nerve-conduction testing records a ≥20% increase in response amplitude relative to the preoperative measurement. This was the published definition of nerve-conduction improvement in NCT01292876. In the 2016 report, eight of 13 participants underwent electrodiagnostic evaluation; subject 8's femoral motor response increased from 3.8 to 5.0 millivolts. The measurement establishes improved electrical responsiveness without attributing it specifically to newly formed fibres.
milestones.set_by: University of Pittsburgh, NCT01292876, electrodiagnostic outcome definition published by Dziki et al. (2016).
milestones.threshold_quote: Improvement in nerve conduction was defined as a ⩾20% increase in motor nerve conduction amplitude.

milestones.title: A patient with VML gains at least 25% over the presurgical functional maximum.
milestones.criterion: After preoperative rehabilitation reaches a plateau, a treated VML patient exceeds the presurgical functional maximum by ≥25%, the positive-responder definition in NCT01292876. The five-patient report published on 30 April 2014 classified two patients as nonresponders. The later XenMatrix AB study, NCT04051242, consented 10 people, implanted two and obtained one six-month assessment; its results were posted on 25 April 2025 and were not peer reviewed. Neither study establishes controlled efficacy.
milestones.set_by: University of Pittsburgh, NCT01292876, positive-responder criterion published by Sicari et al. (2014); specific to that clinical protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: a 25% or greater increase over their presurgical functional maximum.

milestones.title: A controlled human study attributes voluntary force to muscle regenerated within a VML defect.
milestones.criterion: One registered, controlled human study demonstrates perfused, motor-innervated muscle within a VML defect producing voluntary force through its attachments at the final follow-up after rehabilitation. The result distinguishes force from regenerated tissue from compensation by surviving muscle. This is the first-study result preceding independent replication. The 2016 cohort did not establish a causal relationship between new muscle and functional improvement.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of ASTM F3645-25, USAMMDA/MTEC targets and registered VML studies found no published criterion for this controlled human demonstration.

not_found: No registered controlled human study directly attributing recovered voluntary force to regenerated VML muscle was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov's primary results pages and the posted NCT04051242 protocol PDF did not expose readable text; the study's results were readable in a registry mirror.
Greising and Call's full review could not be reopened through its DOI, Wiley or PubMed Central.
